text: Missing values are easy to spot because they show up as NaN. Duplicates and inconsistent spellings are sneakier — the data looks complete, but totals are inflated and groups are split apart. If you've written select distinct, or group by with having count star greater than 1, in T-SQL, you already know the goal. This lesson shows the pandas tools for it.

Here's a small illustrative orders table with six rows. Orders dot duplicated dot sum comes back as 1 — duplicated compares all columns by default and marks only the second and later copies of an exact match, so just one row gets flagged here. Orders dot drop underscore duplicates removes it and keeps the first occurrence.

In practice, duplicate usually means the same business key, not identical in every column. Pass subset equal to order underscore id, and now two rows get flagged instead of one — the copy of order 5002, and the second row of order 5004. Order 5004 is the interesting one: its amounts actually differ, 200 versus 210, so it's a conflict, not a copy. Dropping it quietly means guessing which value is right.

To see every row involved in a conflict, not just the later ones, use keep equals False — that shows both rows of order 5004 side by side so you can actually compare them. If you must resolve it automatically, keep equals first, the default, or keep equals last, chooses a winner — only do this when you actually know the later row is the corrected one, for example when rows are sorted by load time.

Now a customer table where the same information gets written several different ways. Value underscore counts on the state column shows G-A once, Georgia once, lowercase g-a once, and G-A with a trailing space once — one real state, four different values. A groupby on state here would give you four separate groups, none of them complete.

Use the dot-s-t-r methods from the previous chapter to fix this. Strip and title-case the name column, collapsing any double spaces with a regex replace along the way. Strip and uppercase the state column, then replace Georgia with G-A using a dictionary. Lowercase the status column too. After this, value underscore counts on state shows G-A at a clean 4, and both Ana Ruiz rows now share the exact same spelling, so drop underscore duplicates correctly recognizes them as the same person.

The order here really matters. First, strip and normalize case, so spelling differences vanish entirely. Second, map variants with a dictionary for values like Georgia that need an actual translation, not just a case fix. Third, deduplicate, now that identical records actually look identical to pandas. And fourth, verify with value underscore counts and a before-and-after row count, so you know exactly what each step removed.

To recap: duplicated flags repeats, drop underscore duplicates removes them, subset defines the key, and keep picks the survivor. Exact copies are safe to drop; conflicting duplicates need real investigation first. Inconsistent spellings split groups — fix them with strip, upper or lower, and dictionary replacements. Standardize first, deduplicate second, verify last. Next: data type problems and parsing.
